presenterNotes: Start with the Property of Equality for Exponential Equations as the core idea. Everything else—rewriting bases, using negative exponents, graphing—are strategies to apply this property.
When teaching rewriting bases, use a 'cheat sheet' of common powers (2^2=4, 2^3=8, 3^2=9, 3^3=27, 5^2=25, 5^3=125, etc.) so students can quickly recognize them.
Graphing is a powerful fallback. Emphasize that if they can't find a common base, they should immediately think 'graph it'.
The blueprint ties the methods together. Help students see that the Understand phase determines the entire solution path.

discoveryHook.scenario: When two powers with the same base are equal, their exponents must be equal. It's like two runners on identical tracks—if they finish at the same spot, they must have started at the same time. This simple idea lets you solve exponential equations instantly!

explanation: An [[kw:exponential equation]] has variable expressions in the exponent(s).
The [[kw:Property of Equality for Exponential Equations]]: If $b > 0$, $b \neq 1$, and $b^x = b^y$, then $x = y$.
To solve, rewrite each side as a power of the [[imp:same base]], then set the exponents equal.
If the bases are already the same, simply equate the exponents and solve the resulting linear equation.
Always check your solution by substituting back into the original equation.

notes: The bases must be exactly the same.
If the bases are different, try to rewrite them as powers of the same base.
formulaCard.title: Property of Equality for Exponential Equations
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{If } b^x = b^y \text{ and } b>0, b\neq 1, \text{ then } x = y. $$

teacherCues: Write $3^{x+1} = 3^5$ on the board and ask: 'Since the bases are the same, what must be true about the exponents?'
State the Property of Equality for Exponential Equations: If $b^x = b^y$, then $x = y$ (for $b>0, b\neq 1$).

confusionCorner.body: The property only works when $b > 0$ and $b \neq 1$. If $b = 1$, then $1^x = 1^y$ is true for all $x, y$, so you cannot equate exponents. If $b$ is negative, the equation may have no solution or multiple solutions.
confusionCorner.title: Base Must Be Positive and Not 1

questions.feedbackIfWrong: If the bases are equal and positive (not 1), then the exponents must be equal, so $x = y$.

explanation: If bases are different, rewrite each side as a power of the [[imp:same base]].
Look for common bases: 4, 8, 16 can be written as powers of 2; 9, 27, 81 as powers of 3.
Use the properties of exponents (Power of a Power) to simplify.
Once the bases are the same, equate the exponents and solve.
Fractions like $\frac{1}{2}$ can be rewritten as $2^{-1}$; $\frac{1}{64}$ as $4^{-3}$ or $2^{-6}$, etc.

confusionCorner.title: Choosing the Right Base
confusionCorner.body: Not all numbers share an obvious common base. If you can't find one, you may need to solve by graphing. Always try the smallest base first (2, 3, 5).

blocks.title: Solving Exponential Equations with Unlike Bases

discoveryHook.scenario: When bases don't match, think of them as different costumes on the same actor. If you can rewrite both sides as powers of the same number, the costumes come off and you can compare the actors—the exponents—directly. It's a base disguise party!

blocks.title: Solving When Bases Are Fractions

discoveryHook.scenario: Fractions like $\frac{1}{2}$ or $\frac{1}{8}$ are just powers with negative exponents. By rewriting them, you turn a scary fraction into a familiar integer base. Suddenly, the equation becomes a friendly same-base problem!

formulaCard.title: Negative Exponent Rewrite
notes: Always convert fractions to a base with a negative exponent.
Then use Power of a Power to simplify.

explanation: Fractions can be expressed as powers using [[imp:negative exponents]]: $\frac{1}{b} = b^{-1}$, $\frac{1}{b^n} = b^{-n}$.
Rewrite the fraction as a power of the base, then use the Property of Equality for Exponential Equations.
This is especially useful when the base is a fraction like $1/2$, $1/3$, etc., and the other side is a power of the reciprocal.
Remember: $a^{-n} = \frac{1}{a^n}$ and $\frac{1}{a^{-n}} = a^n$.

teacherCues: Write $(1/2)^x = 4$ and ask: 'How can we rewrite 1/2 as a power of 2?'
Guide: $1/2 = 2^{-1}$. Then use Power of a Power.

explanation: When an exponential equation cannot be rewritten with the same base, solve by graphing.
Write a system: $y_1 = $ left side, $y_2 = $ right side.
Graph both functions on a graphing calculator.

The $x$-coordinate is the solution. Exponential equations can have 0, 1, or multiple solutions.

notes: Always check for extraneous solutions if the base involves variables.
Use technology for graphing to get precise answers.

rows.2: Identify the common base and rewrite each side.
Equate exponents and solve the linear equation.
State solution; check in original equation.

explanation: The blueprint for exponential equations: [[imp:Understand]] – Examine the bases. Are they already the same? Can they be rewritten to be the same? If not, plan to graph.
[[imp:Solve]] – If bases can be matched, rewrite using exponent properties, equate exponents, and solve. If not, graph and find the intersection.
[[imp:Conclude]] – State the solution. If solved algebraically, check by substituting into the original equation. If graphing, verify the $x$-value is reasonable.

confusionCorner.body: Even when bases can be matched, graphing provides a visual check. If you're unsure of your algebraic solution, graph both sides and see if the intersection matches your answer.
confusionCorner.title: Graphing is Always an Option

discoveryHook.scenario: With the Understand → Solve → Conclude blueprint, you have a plan for any exponential equation. Understand the bases—can they match? Solve by equating exponents or by graphing. Conclude with the solution and a quick check. This blueprint makes you an exponential equation expert!
